questions.q: What is the mandatory attribute for the tag that provides alternative text for screen readers and broken images?
questions.a: The mandatory attribute is `alt`. A wrong answer (e.g., "src" or "title") reveals the student confuses the image source with accessibility requirement. The `alt` attribute is required by HTML5 validation and WCAG guidelines; omitting it makes the page inaccessible to visually impaired users.

questions.q:
Explain why the following nested list code is invalid: `
  • Fruits
    • Apple
  • Vegetables
` — actually it IS valid. Now explain why this code is invalid: `
  • Fruits
    • Apple
  • Vegetables
`
questions.a: The second code is invalid because the nested `<ul>` is a direct child of the outer `<ul>`, not wrapped inside an `<li>`. In HTML, lists can only contain `<li>` elements (and for `<dl>`, `<dt>`/`<dd>`). A wrong answer (e.g., "nesting not allowed") reveals the student doesn't understand that nesting must occur *inside* a list item, not between list items.

questions.q: Write the HTML to display a 3×3 table where the top-left cell spans two columns and contains "Header", the next cell in row 1 is "Marks", and row 2 has three data cells: "Maths", "90", "A". Use only table tags (no CSS).
questions.a:
```html
Header Marks
Maths 90 A
``` A wrong answer (e.g., using `colspan="3"` or missing ``) reveals the student doesn't grasp that `colspan` counts columns *in that row*, and that header cells (``) are semantically distinct from data cells (``).

questions.q:
Compare the rendering and semantic meaning of `
HTML
HyperText Markup Language
` vs `
  • HTML: HyperText Markup Language
`. When should you choose one over the other?
questions.a: `<dl>` (description list) semantically groups term-definition pairs, enabling screen readers to announce "term: definition" relationships. `<ul>` is for unordered items without explicit label-value structure. Choose `<dl>` for glossaries, metadata, FAQs; choose `<ul>` for simple bullet points. A wrong answer (e.g., "they look the same") reveals the student focuses only on visual output, not semantic accessibility.

questions.q: A student sets `width="200"` and `height="150"` on an `` whose actual file is 400×300 pixels. Evaluate: does this reduce page load time? Justify.
questions.a: No. The browser still downloads the full 400×300 image file (same bytes), then scales it down for display. Load time is unchanged; only rendering changes. To reduce load time, the image file itself must be resized/compressed server-side. A wrong answer ("yes, smaller dimensions = smaller file") reveals the common confusion between display size and file size.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: HTML images, lists, and tables are structural elements used to embed media, organize information sequentially or ______, and present tabular data in rows and columns respectively, enabling meaningful content layout on web pages.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're building a class ______ webpage for your school.
What is HTML images, lists, and tables? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: HTML images, lists, and tables are structural elements used to embed media, organize information sequentially or hierarchically, and present tabular data in rows and columns respectively, enabling meaningful content layout on web pages.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: "How do I make a grid where 'Monday' spans ______ periods?" → leads to table with colspan.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about HTML images, lists, and tables?

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can independently write valid HTML code to: (1) insert an image with proper src, alt, width, and height attributes; (2) create nested ordered/unordered lists with correct nesting syntax; (3) build a data table using <table>, <tr>, <th>, <td> with rowspan/colspan for merged cells; and (4) explain the accessibility purpose of alt.
